Strains over the big-power veto showed up early at the United Nations. Resolution 40 was passed on 13 December 1946. It notes the rows that had grown up around Article 27 of the Charter. That clause gives the five permanent members of the Security Council their veto. Small states feared the veto would slow the Council or block it outright.

The Assembly begs the permanent members to take care, in talks with each other and with fellow members, that the veto not bar swift Council action. It also urges the Council to adopt habits of work, within the Charter, that ease the strain. The veto fight, as this text shows, is as old as the UN itself.
un-ga-res-140:
Nauru, a tiny island in the Pacific Ocean, passed from League of Nations rule to UN trusteeship under Resolution 140, adopted on 1 November 1947. Under the old League mandate, Australia had run the island on behalf of itself, New Zealand, and the United Kingdom. The UN Charter of 1945 had since set up a Trusteeship System for just such lands.

The three states agreed to place Nauru under that system and to run it on the terms set out here. The Assembly, acting under Article 85 of the Charter, approves those terms in place of the old mandate. Nauru stayed a trust land for two more decades, until its freedom in 1968.
un-ga-res-a-69-40:

It argues that the spread of these arms in any form would deepen the risk of nuclear war. Full nuclear disarmament, and the end of such arms for good, are held up as the sole sure guard.

Till that day comes, states with nuclear arms are pressed to shield states without them from use or threat of use. The hair-trigger alert of ready arms is singled out: it carries an unfit risk of a launch by error or without leave, with ruin for all mankind.

Michael Forgber, Rajatava Basu, Kaushik Roychoudhury, and co-authors mapped what the immune system sees during a parasitic infection in 2006. Leishmania donovani causes visceral leishmaniasis, a deadly disease spread by sand flies. Antigenicity is the measure of which parasite proteins the human immune system actually attacks.

Using proteome serology, testing patient blood serum against the parasite's full set of proteins, the team mapped those targets across the proteome. A map of what the body recognizes is a shortlist for vaccines and for blood tests that could diagnose the disease early. For a neglected illness of the poor, that shortlist is where practical defenses begin.

frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d140: General Eisenhower wrote to President Roosevelt on November 18, 1943, and his letter is Document 140 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d240:
Secretary of State Cordell Hull sent President Roosevelt a long secret digest from Washington on 20 November 1943, gathering reports from Ankara, Algiers, and Madrid. It is a snapshot of half a dozen side issues of the war in a single message.

British and Turkish officers, Ankara reports, differ wildly on Axis striking power against Turkey, and a compromise estimate will set the aid Turkey needs. From Algiers come orders to hold German prisoners accused of atrocities for later trial, and news of Yugoslav partisans interned on the Italian mainland. Madrid reports a protest over the many German agents working in Spain. It also reports pressure to shut the German consulate at Tangier. Washington wishes to let the Laurel incident rest if Spain proves itself by deeds.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d340:
A draft agreement prepared by the American delegation at Cairo on 30 November 1943, marked secret, sets the liaison rules between the European Advisory Commission and the Combined Chiefs of Staff. It grew out of John McCloy's talks with Eden, and its heading shows it was accepted at the Sextant Conference.

The Moscow conference had created the commission and sent it civil affairs questions closely tied to military matters of prime interest to the chiefs. Under the draft, the commission's tentative recommendations go to the chiefs for comment before final submission to the three governments. Approved recommendations return to the chiefs, who prepare the final directives for commanders in the field. British members of the civil affairs committee are to take full part in all its work, without limit as to area.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d440:
Agreed minutes, signed off by both the American and British sides, record a United States-United Kingdom meeting of December 4, 1943, during the Second Cairo Conference. Unlike a single nation's notes, an agreed text is the version both delegations accepted as accurate. The State Department printed it in the Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

Inside, the reader finds the shared record of what the two allies discussed and settled that day, in the middle of a conference called to finish the work begun at Tehran. Agreed minutes carry special weight for historians, because neither side could later rewrite them. They mark the points where London and Washington truly stood together.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d540:

Harriman's Moscow embassy was then Washington's main window on the Soviet Union. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

Harriman wrote to Hull on departmental business and to Roosevelt on the great questions, and the choice of channel itself is a clue to a message's weight. Six weeks after Tehran, Soviet-American relations were entering their working phase. For readers, this cable shows the alliance being run through proper diplomatic form as well as summit friendship.
frus-1944-quebec-d40:
Wilson Brown, the President's naval aide, wrote to A. J. McFarland, secretary of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, on August 31, 1944. Brown managed the President's military household and map room. The message appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

Staff traffic between the White House military office and the Joint Chiefs' secretariat arranged the soldiers' part of the coming conference: papers, attendance, and the movement of plans. Brown and McFarland were the kind of officers whose names rarely reach print but whose work made summits run. For readers, the note shows a conference's military skeleton being assembled.
frus-1944-quebec-d140:
Numbered C.C.S. 654, this top-secret memorandum from the United States Chiefs of Staff is dated August 22, 1944. It proposes the basic policies the Combined Chiefs should adopt for the next Anglo-American staff conference, the meeting that became the Quebec Conference. The paper states the coalition's whole strategy in a few numbered paragraphs.

The over-all objective is the unconditional surrender of the Axis, in cooperation with Russia and other allies. Europe comes first; meanwhile pressure on Japan must never slacken. Once Europe is defeated, the full resources of both nations turn on Japan. The listed undertakings include aiding Russia and China, assisting French and Italian forces, and moving troops from Europe to the Pacific as a first priority.
frus-1944-quebec-d240:
Hopkins wrote to Roosevelt on September 13, 1944, about "the Italian business." He had talked with O'Dwyer, Crowley, and the State Department. He urged the president to take the initiative at Quebec. Roosevelt should win Churchill's approval for a course of action announced publicly. The machinery for quick relief and rehabilitation purchases, he said, was already available.

Italians could pay for goods, other than emergency relief, from funds accruing from American soldiers' pay in Italy. Two matters needed clearing up fast: the prisoner of war question, and amendment of the armistice terms. An attached memorandum argues Italy must return quickly to political and economic independence, free from domination by any powerful neighbor, with shipping, trucks, and payment as the immediate problems.

Evelyn Underhill, the scholar who brought mysticism to modern English readers, devoted a full study to Jan van Ruusbroec. Ruusbroec was a fourteenth-century Flemish mystic, among the great voices of medieval Dutch spirituality. Underhill follows him from parish priest to prior of a religious community.

Beyond the life, she explains his vision of the soul's ascent toward God, in language meant for readers outside a monastery. His teaching stressed an active life of love joined to deep contemplation. Underhill treats him not as a curiosity but as a serious guide, and her study remains a short, sympathetic entry into his thought.
tob-13340:
R. H. Charles's classic translation presents the Book of Enoch, an ancient apocalypse attributed to Noah's great-grandfather. Quoted in the New Testament letter of Jude, Enoch was nevertheless left out of most Bibles. Preserved whole only in Ethiopia's canon, the text survived in Ge'ez while its Hebrew and Aramaic forms largely vanished.

Its central story tells of the Watchers, angels who descended for human women, fathered giants, and taught forbidden arts, bringing judgment on heaven and earth. Visions of the end times follow. Enoch shaped early Christian and Jewish ideas of demons, fallen angels, and final judgment more deeply than its excluded status would suggest.

Elias Ashmole, astrologer and collector, saved England's alchemical verse in the Theatrum Chemicum Britannicum of 1652. He printed the poetic pieces of the famous English philosophers of the hermetic art: George Ripley, Thomas Norton, and masters whose names are lost.

The poems teach the Great Work in allegory and riddle, in the spelling and music of their age. Ashmole, whose gifts founded Oxford's Ashmolean Museum, knew these texts might vanish without him. He was right. Checked from the 1919 printing, his collection remains the great storehouse of English alchemy in verse, and a monument to one collector's foresight.
tob-4240:
William Hone, the radical London printer who beat blasphemy charges in famous trials, published his Apocryphal New Testament in 1820. His collection prints the writings the early church left outside its canon. Infancy gospels of Jesus stand here, and the Gospel of Nicodemus. Letters ascribed to Paul and others fill out the set.

Hone meant the book for freethinkers' shelves, and it stayed in print for that audience all century. The translations are old ones, gathered rather than made fresh. Checked from the 1919 printing, his volume shows how apocrypha reached ordinary readers: cheaply, boldly, and under a fighter's imprint.
tob-0040:
Rob Arndt compiled German Disc Programs and Occult Origins, a research file on the claims of Nazi disc aircraft and their supposed occult roots. It treats the Haunebu and Vril craft of postwar legend and the Thule and Vril societies of early Nazi lore. The work dates from 2016 and circulates as a fringe-history dossier.

Arndt gathers the saucer stories, secret-society genealogies, and wonder-weapon tales into one documented survey of the mythos. No reliable evidence supports the disc programs as real aircraft; historians class them as postwar legend. The compilation's value lies in showing the legend whole: how occult societies, wartime rumor, and flying-saucer culture fused into a lasting story.
stukeley-stonehenge-temple-restord-1740:
Antiquary William Stukeley surveyed Stonehenge and read it as a Druid temple. His book Stonehenge, A Temple Restor'd to the British Druids came out in 1740. Stukeley was a doctor and cleric who loved old Britain.

He measured the stones and the avenues around them with care. Then he built a grand theory of Druid rites upon the plan. That theory is now doubted, but his records hold real value. Later diggers destroyed much that he drew in place. His dream of Druids shaped how Britain saw the stones for two centuries.
vyse-operations-pyramids-gizeh-vol-1-184:
Richard William Howard Vyse blasted his way into the Great Pyramid in 1837, and Vol. 1 of his Operations, out in 1840, tells how. Vyse was a chief of troops with funds and zeal. With the aid of Perring, he forced the hid rooms past the king's hall. There he found the name of Khufu writ in red paint.

That find fixed who built the heap for good. Logs, costs, and tales of the dig crowd the tome. His rough means drew scorn, yet his finds changed the field. This is the first full tale of a dig there.
vyse-operations-pyramids-gizeh-vol-2-184:
Richard William Howard Vyse pushed his dig past the great heap in Vol. 2 of his Operations, out in 1840. The first tome told of the forced rooms and the name of Khufu. Here the work spreads to the next heaps, the Sphinx, and tombs in the sand. Perring's fine plans and cuts fill page past page.

Those plans are the tome's chief worth. Digs since then still cite their sums and lines. The log prose is dry, yet the scale of the work stuns. Read as a pair, the tomes found the dig of the heaps.
machiavelli-prince-dacres-1640:
Niccolò Machiavelli wrote The Prince in Italian, and Edward Dacres made the first English version in 1640. Dacres gave English readers Machiavelli's masterpiece a century after it stirred Italy in print there. The slim book of counsel on power still starts fights about ends and means.

Machiavelli tells a new prince how to gain a state and keep it by force. Fear, he argues, beats love when a ruler must choose, and cruelty has its uses. He praises Cesare Borgia's ruthless craft and blames mercy that breeds disorder in a state. Fox and lion, fraud and force, are his paired tools of rule in the text. The name Machiavellian for cold statecraft starts with this blunt little book's fame.
lermontov-hero-of-our-time-1840:
Mikhail Lermontov published A Hero of Our Time in 1840, a Russian novel made of five linked tales. The hero is Pechorin, a young officer serving in the Caucasus. He is clever, bored, and often cruel to those who love him. Other narrators describe him before his own diary speaks.

The tales include a kidnapping, a smugglers' plot, a duel, and a wager on fate. Pechorin treats life as a game and leaves harm behind him. Lermontov died young, yet this book secured his fame. It gave Russian fiction one of its first great antiheroes and a sharp portrait of a restless generation.
ranke-history-popes-vol-1-1840:
Leopold von Ranke's History of the Popes, Volume 1, appears in Sarah Austin's translation of 1840. Ranke is called the father of modern historiography for his use of archives. This volume covers the papacy from its medieval height through the Reformation era. Popes, cardinals, and Italian courts come alive from state papers.

Ranke aimed to show the past as it actually was, in his famous phrase. His calm tone toward Catholic and Protestant alike was new and striking. The work made the seminar method of history famous abroad. Austin's version carried it through the English-speaking world. Volume 1 opens a classic of both church and political history.
whitefield-journals-1740:
George Whitefield was the most famous preacher of the eighteenth century, whose voice could reach crowds in open fields. His Journals, first published in 1740, record his preaching tours across Britain and America in his own words. Whitefield wrote them partly to answer his critics.

He describes packed churches, weeping hearers, journeys by horse and ship, and his break with John Wesley over doctrine. The entries mix frank self-praise with real wonder at the crowds his message drew. Historians of the Great Awakening treat the Journals as a prime source written from the movement's center.
shelley-defence-of-poetry-1840:
Percy Bysshe Shelley wrote A Defence of Poetry in 1821, answering a friend's playful claim that poetry was fading in a practical age. Shelley left the essay unfinished, and it stayed in manuscript until 1840. By then Shelley had been dead for eighteen years.

Shelley argues that poets shape the moral and social imagination of their age. Reason counts and measures, he says, but imagination gives knowledge its human worth. Poetry strengthens sympathy, the root of all moral good. The essay closes with the famous claim that poets are the unacknowledged legislators of the world. It became the most quoted defense of poetry of the whole century.
cooper-pathfinder-1840:
James Fenimore Cooper returned to Leatherstocking after a long break and published The Pathfinder in 1840. He set it on Lake Ontario during the Seven Years' War, when his hero is in his prime as a scout. Cooper had always insisted Natty needed a love story, and this is the volume that gives him one.

Natty, called Pathfinder for his unerring woodcraft, guides young Mabel Dunham to her father's island fort. He falls quietly in love with her, though a dashing rival and his own honest nature stand in the way. French and Indian attacks, a blockade, and a storm on the lake supply the action. Cooper's lake scenery is among his finest writing. The Pathfinder is the essential middle volume of the Leatherstocking Tales.
townshend-facts-in-mesmerism-1840:
Chauncy Hare Townshend made the literary case for mesmerism in Facts in Mesmerism, printed in 1840. Townshend was a poet and man of letters, not a doctor. His book records cases he witnessed and tested himself. The subtitle pleads for a dispassionate inquiry into the subject.

He asks readers to weigh evidence before they mock or believe. Mesmeric sleep, painless operations, and clairvoyant claims enter his record. The work became the most cited early English defense outside medical journals. It shows mesmerism winning cultured friends in its first British years. Townshend's tone is curious, candid, and measured. His cases still anchor histories of the movement.
plos-pone-0003440:
Peter V. Lovell and colleagues read gene activity in the songbird brain in this 2008 paper. Songbirds learn their songs, much as children learn speech. A set of brain nuclei, called the song system, drives that learning. The team used high-throughput methods to profile genes across that system.

The profiles revealed chemical specializations in the song nuclei. Certain signals and receptors stood out against the rest of the brain. Those traits may support vocal learning, a rare skill among animals. The results offer clues to the molecular basis of learned song and speech.
plos-pone-0003540:
Tetsuya Kimura and co-authors studied an enzyme tied to memory in this 2008 paper. GSK-3β is an enzyme suspected in Alzheimer's disease. That disease starts with memory disturbance in its early stages. The enzyme's normal role in the adult brain was not well understood.

The team showed GSK-3β is required for memory reconsolidation. That process restabilizes a memory after it is recalled. Blocking the enzyme kept recalled memories from settling again. The finding names a molecular step in how memories persist. Recalled memories are not fixed files, and this work shows one way they shift.
plos-pone-0003640:
Till Bärnighausen, Claudia Wallrauch, Alex Welte, and colleagues published this methods study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Counting new HIV infections is hard, so surveys use a blood test meant to flag recent ones. The team checked that test, called cBED, in rural South Africa.

They compared incidence estimates from one-time survey testing with estimates from following the same population over years. There was concern the assay wrongly classifies some long-standing infections as recent, inflating the count. The head-to-head check shows how far the shortcut can be trusted for planning HIV programs.
plos-pone-0003740:
Dimitrios Iliopoulos, Konstantinos N. Malizos, Pagona Oikonomou, and colleagues published this arthritis study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Osteoarthritis wears down joint cartilage and affects more than 100 million people worldwide. Its causes mix genes, mechanics, and environment, and its gene list was incomplete.

The team combined microRNA data with proteomic data, the full set of proteins in tissue. Together the two approaches flagged new osteoarthritis genes. They also mapped how the hits work together in metabolic and inflammatory networks, showing the disease as a joint effort of many genes. Worn joints are a top cause of pain in older adults.
plos-pone-0003840:

The pattern recognition approach borrows tumor-antigen hunting for the fight against TB, aiming at better tests and vaccine targets.
plos-pone-0003940:

Their PLOS ONE article removed Pten at set times in the mouse prostate. The pace of early abnormal growth depended on when the gene was cut. Early lesions grew at rates set by that timing. The work shows the order of gene losses shapes how prostate cancer starts.
plos-pone-0004040:
Manos Tsakiris asked how we know a mirror face is our own in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. A reflection looks like us, but looks may not be the whole story. The reflection also moves when we move. We see it touched exactly when we feel touch ourselves.

The study tested how current multisensory input alters self-face recognition. Matching sight and touch cues shifted judgments of what counts as self. That shows self-recognition is built live from several senses. The work informs research on body ownership and its disorders. It appeared in PLOS ONE, and the full text is free for any reader to check.
plos-pone-0004140:
Richard Cudney-Bueno and colleagues published this marine study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Marine reserves, sea areas where fishing is banned, are promoted around the world as tools for conservation and fishery management. Supporters argue that reserves protect sea life and also help fisheries, as extra adults spill out and larvae drift into fishing grounds.

Solid proof for those benefits, especially the larval route, had been thin. The authors present evidence that reserves can produce rapid effects through the spread of larvae to nearby waters. Their findings support the idea that a reserve can repay nearby fisheries quickly, not just in the long run.
plos-pone-0004240:

The team studied mice lacking KRAP and fed them a fattening diet. They report altered energy homeostasis and resistance to diet-induced obesity in these mice. A protein that, when missing, keeps mice lean on rich food is a clue to how the body sets its weight.
plos-pone-0004340:

They derive two candidate ancestral codes, one built from codons of the type RNY, purine, any base, pyrimidine, plus related codons. They argue the modern code keeps vestiges of critical scale invariance from that RNA world in current prokaryote genomes. The code itself, on this view, is a fossil.

plos-pone-0004540: In 2009, Stavrum, Myneedu, and Arora fingerprinted Delhi's TB strains anew. In-depth molecular characterization of Mycobacterium tuberculosis from New Delhi was done. plos-pone-0004640: In 2009, Hans, Kaslin, and Freudenreich brought timed gene switches to fish anew. A time-controlled gene switch worked in zebrafish. The trusty Cre tool worked in fish well. The neat tool aids fish gene research. The timing control is on demand.
plos-pone-0004740: In 2009, Young and a team weighed luck versus law in cichlid evolution anew. Shape diversity in African cichlid radiations came from contingency, chance, and determinism. The three forces all counted here today. The study maps burst radiation patterns. The patterns are compared.
dupotet-cours-magnetisme-sept-lecons-184:
Jules Dupotet teaches animal magnetism in seven lessons in his Cours de magnetisme, in French from 1840. The leading French magnetizer of his day instructs step by step. Students learn how to induce the trance, what signs to expect, and how the magnetic cure claims to heal the sick.

Clear, practical, and fully confident, the course served as the textbook of high mesmerism. Dupotet writes as a master sure of his art and its laws. Passes, rapport, and somnambulism each get their ordered place here. The book shows mesmerism as a teachable craft in its prime, the standard course by which a generation of magnetizers learned their trade.
dupotet-magnetisme-oppose-medecine-1840:
Dupotet declares war on the doctors in Le magnetisme oppose a la medecine, in French from 1840. The magnetic cure, he argues, heals where learned physicians fail. Regular medicine answers with scorn, and the pamphlet war between the schools burns hot on every page of his polemic.

Combative, earnest, and utterly sure of itself, the book speaks for the magnetizers' cause. Dupotet mocks degrees, latin, and fees with a pamphleteer's glee. Patients' cures are his chosen weapons in the fight. The work stands as a founding manifesto of alternative healing in nineteenth-century France, a shot in a long war over who may heal.
mueller-handbuch-physiologie-1840:
Johannes Muller sums up the science of the body in his Handbuch der Physiologie, in German from 1840. The handbook served as the nineteenth century's bible of physiology. Senses, blood, nerves, and voice all fall under Muller's vast and orderly learning, drawn from his Berlin lectures and his own tireless trials.

His students included Helmholtz, Virchow, and Du Bois-Reymond, founders of modern medicine in their turn. Muller taught them to test every claim on living tissue. Few teachers have ever shaped a science so deeply through pupils. The book stands behind a whole era of German medicine, the seedbed from which its golden age grew.
teste-manuel-pratique-magnetisme-1840:
Alphonse Teste wrote his Practical Manual of Animal Magnetism in French in 1840. French healers who used magnetic passes and trance soon treated it as their standard guide. Teste aimed to make a disputed art look calm, skilled, and safe.

Step by step, the manual shows how to induce a trance in a patient. It then explains how to read illness during magnetic sleep and how to treat it. Clear rules, case notes, and warnings fill the pages. The book shows what a trained magnetizer in France was expected to know and do each day.
savigny-system-heutigen-roem-rechts-1840:
Savigny's System of Modern Roman Law began appearing in German in 1840, the summa of his career. He had led the historical school for a quarter century, and the System gathers its doctrine into one ordered account of private law. Lawyers call the approach pandectist, after the Pandects, the Roman Digest at its core.

The volumes order the whole of private law: persons, property, obligations, and family, each concept defined and placed by historical light. Savigny's method treats law as a system whose parts explain each other, growing from a people's life rather than a legislator's whim. The System became the bible of nineteenth-century jurisprudence in Germany. Its concepts passed into the German Civil Code of 1900, so its fingerprints rest on the private law of many nations today.
cia-0000007540:

A heading in the issue points to intelligence treated in recent publications, a sign officers tracked outside writing about their field. The journal's readers were practitioners, not the general public.

Pages like these record a profession pausing to examine itself: its books, its methods, and its mistakes. That habit matters because secret work rarely gets open debate. Now declassified, the issue helps historians see what concerned American analysts as the Vietnam War widened. The text survives through the CIA reading room release.
cia-0000008640:
A crashed US Air Force F-105 was sighted in Hai Hung province, North Vietnam, in a report dated July 1973. The F-105 Thunderchief flew many of the war's hardest bombing missions over the north. Hai Hung lies in the Red River plain east of Hanoi.

By mid-1973 American combat flights had stopped, so wreck sightings mostly aided the accounting for lost crews. A located crash site could confirm what happened to a pilot who never returned. The report shows that work proceeding through local observation after the ceasefire. It is one entry in the air war's long final ledger.

Planners needed prison locations marked clearly, not least so bombs would not fall on captives. Strike reports, meanwhile, recorded what air attacks had done nearby. Holding both subjects together shows the terrible closeness of bombing and captivity in Laos. The file preserves that tension in a single dated record.

Lao-held prisons rarely drew the attention given to American cases. Yet mapping them showed the war's full carceral reach inside Laos itself. Local inmates' fates also tested which side controlled the countryside. This file keeps a Lao prison, not an American one, on the permanent official record.

It also fixed a target for watching in a country officially at peace. The file stands early in the record of Cambodia's hidden role in the prison war.

cia-0000049140: Reporting requirements, the rules for how officers in the field had to file their reports, fill a CIA item from 1989. David L. Reed, Vincent S. Smith, Shaless L. Hammond, and their team read human history from lice in PLOS Biology in 2004. Body lice live in clothing and feed on people. Their genes carry a record of their hosts' past, since lice pass from person to person by close contact.

The genetic data suggest body lice spread at a time that fits direct contact between modern and archaic humans. That is, our ancestors likely met Neandertal-like groups closely enough to share parasites. Clothing use also enters the story, since body lice need garments to live in. The study is a clever use of a humble bug as a witness to events no fossil can show directly.
plos-pone-0000140:
Stuart H. M. Butchart, H. Resit Akçakaya, Janice Chanson, and colleagues published this conservation paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It proposes improvements to the Red List Index. The index is built from the IUCN Red List and tracks how extinction risk changes over time for whole groups of species.

Governments use the index to judge whether conservation is working. The authors address weaknesses in how the index is calculated and sampled. A more reliable index means policy makers can tell real progress from noise. Scarce conservation money can then go where the trend data says it counts.
plos-pone-0000240:
Shoshi Dorfberger, Esther Adi-Japha, and Avi Karni published this motor learning study in PLOS ONE in 2007. When people practice a movement, the memory of it becomes firm over hours, a process called consolidation, but new learning can interfere. The authors found reduced susceptibility to that interference in children before adolescence.

Young learners may hold onto a new motor skill more stubbornly than adults do. The authors compare consolidation in children and adults after training. The result bears on how physical skills, from handwriting to sports, are best taught at different ages, and on rehabilitation after injury.
plos-pone-0000340:
Bita Sehat, Sandra Andersson, Radu Vasilcanu, and colleagues published this cell signaling paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. The IGF-1 receptor receives growth signals and is a target in cancer research. The authors study the role of ubiquitination, the tagging of proteins for disposal, in how the receptor signals. They also trace how the receptor is then degraded, taken off the cell surface and destroyed.

How long a growth receptor stays active shapes how strongly a cell grows. The disposal tag is part of that timing system. The paper maps ubiquitin's role in the receptor's life cycle, knowledge needed for drugs that aim to shut this pathway down in tumors.
plos-pone-0000440:
Dimitar Dimitrov and colleagues built a brighter tool for watching voltage in living cells, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Their enhanced fluorescent protein voltage sensor glows in response to changes in a cell's electrical state. Nerve and heart cells speak in voltage, so a fast, bright sensor lets researchers watch that speech directly.

The team engineered the protein and characterized how well it works. Genetic voltage sensors can be aimed at chosen cell types, something electrodes cannot easily do. Improving their brightness and speed opens the way to filming electrical activity across whole circuits, a long-standing goal in neuroscience and cardiology.
plos-pone-0000540:
Hiroyuki Yamamoto and colleagues studied antibodies that help keep HIV in check after infection, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Most people's infections run unchecked, but some hold the virus down. Neutralizing antibodies, which block the virus head-on, are prime suspects in that control. The team weighed their role in post-infection control of the virus.

If antibodies made after infection can still rein the virus in, vaccine makers gain a real target. A vaccine could teach the body to make those same antibodies before it ever meets the virus. The study weighs how much of natural control these antibodies can explain, next to other arms of defense.
plos-pone-0000640:
Vinet Coetzee, Louise Barrett, Jaco M. Greeff and co-authors tested a popular idea about faces and genes in PLOS ONE in 2007. HLA genes help the immune system, and three hypotheses link them to health and to facial attractiveness. The proposed routes are avoiding inbreeding, gaining an edge from mixed gene copies, and selection that favors rare types.

Their title states a split result: common HLA alleles were associated with health, but not with facial attractiveness. That weakens the claim that good-looking faces advertise HLA quality. Evolutionary psychologists and geneticists get a careful check on a theory that is often repeated more strongly than the evidence allows.
plos-pone-0000740:
Andrew J. Spiers followed a bacterial mutant's fortunes on a flat world, writing in PLOS ONE in 2007. The Wrinkly Spreader is a bacterium whose altered form succeeds in still liquid cultures by colonizing the air-liquid interface, forming a mat at the surface. Bacterial adaptation often establishes new genotypes with significantly altered traits. Spiers moved the test to two-dimensional agar plates.

His themes are maladaptation, compensation, and ecological success. A trait that wins in liquid may cost its bearer on agar, and later changes may compensate. The microcosm is simple by design: one surface, one mutant, clear outcomes. Evolution experiments like this show adaptation's trade-offs in miniature.
plos-pone-0000840:
John S. Brownstein, Margarita Sordo, Isaac S. Kohane and colleagues asked whether routine health data could have caught a drug danger earlier. COX-2 selective inhibitors, painkillers sold as rofecoxib and celecoxib, are associated with myocardial infarction, heart attack. The team sought to determine whether population health monitoring would have revealed the drugs' effect on population-level patterns of heart attacks.

Their retrospective study used inpatients at two Boston hospitals, as the abstract reports. The playful title, The Tell-Tale Heart, covers a serious method: surveillance of ordinary records as an early warning system for drug safety. If monitoring can spot risk in real time, regulators need not wait for scandals.
plos-pone-0000940:
Godwin Ashiabi and Keri O'Neal modeled how poverty reaches children's health through hardship and parenting, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Low income alone does not tell the whole story of a child's health. Families also face material hardship, trouble paying for food, housing and care, and strain that shapes parenting.

The authors test a model with several paths running at once. They ask how much of poverty's effect travels through hardship and family factors. Answers like this decide where help does most good: raising income, easing hardship or supporting parents. The study treats child health as the end of a chain, not a single cause.
plos-pone-0001040:
Andrew Oxman, Signe Flottorp, Kari Havelserud and colleagues ran a televised, web based trial of valerian for insomnia, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The trial was part of a project to help the public use research in health decisions. Viewers could join the study and follow the process through television and the web.

Valerian is an herbal remedy widely taken for poor sleep. In a randomised trial, participants received valerian or a comparison under that public format. The design itself is the experiment's second subject: can open, broadcast trials recruit well and stay rigorous. Sleep remedies are a fair first case, since demand and doubt are both high.
plos-pone-0001240:
Eating less and dampening insulin signaling are two regimens that extend life in many organisms. Wendy Iser and Catherine Wolkow asked how the two interact in the worm C. elegans, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Genetic analysis had shown that dietary restriction and reduced insulin-like signaling work through distinct pathways in the worm.

The authors report that DAF-2, the worm's insulin-like receptor, modifies the effects of dietary restriction and nutrient stress on aging, stress resistance, and growth. Even distinct pathways talk to each other. Their results shape how combined interventions for aging might behave.
plos-pone-0001340:
To replicate, lentiviruses such as HIV must insert DNA copies of their genomes into host chromosomes. Heather Marshall and colleagues studied a host protein, PSIP1, also called LEDGF/p75, that guides that insertion, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Lentiviral integration is favored in active transcription units, which allows efficient viral gene expression after integration.

The authors examine the role of PSIP1/LEDGF/p75 in lentiviral infectivity and integration targeting. A host factor the virus depends on is a tempting drug target, because the virus cannot easily mutate its way around it. Their work clarifies how much of integration this factor controls.
plos-pone-0001440:
Danielle Kemmer and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE paper on a score for how well a gene is known. Labs know a lot about some genes and near nothing about others. There was no plain scale for that gap. The team built a score that rates how deep the notes on each protein coding gene run.

Their score is drawn from text and data on what each gene does. It mirrors how people judge a gene as known or obscure. A scale like this can steer funds to the least known genes. It can also track how fast the gene map as a whole is being filled in.
plos-pone-0001540:
Der-Chih Yang and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how stem cells choose fat or bone. Stem cells from marrow can become fat cells, bone cells, and more. Fat and bone fates pull against each other, but the control was vague. The team tested a cell signal path that runs through a common messenger.

They show this path steers both fates and sets the mix of two bone signals. It works in part by curbing the hormone leptin. A single path that tips the fat bone balance has clear clinical pull. It may bear on bone loss and weight gain in aging.
plos-pone-0001640:
Emmanuel S. Onaivi and co-authors reviewed what is known about CB2 cannabinoid receptors in the brain in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. These receptors respond to cannabis-like compounds. Addiction and major depression are the health problems in view; both are tied to stress and both often return after treatment.

Many labs had failed to find CB2 receptors in healthy brains, which made their role in mood and drug use an open dispute. Onaivi and his team pull together evidence from mouse work and human subjects on where these receptors occur and what they do. The full text weighs the detection methods and the case for CB2 as a drug target. If the receptors do act in the brain, blocking or boosting them could offer a new route to treat addiction and depression.
plos-pone-0001740:
Corinne Vacher, Dominique Piou, and Marie-Laure Desprez-Loustau analyzed a network of tree diseases in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Ecological networks often show compartments and nestedness, patterns whose causes are debated. The authors used a well-resolved network of host and pathogen interactions to find what shapes them. They drew on a long forest health survey from 1972 to 2005.

Their paper asks how past evolutionary history asymmetrically influences the antagonistic tree and fungus network. The full text gives the network maps and the tests of compartment structure. Knowing whether pathogens cluster by host family history helps foresters predict which trees a new disease can jump to. That is a pressing question as tree pathogens spread worldwide.
plos-pone-0001840:
Michael J. Proulx, Petra Stoerig, Eva Ludowig, and their co-authors tested a device that lets blind people 'see' through sound in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Sensory substitution devices translate inaccessible visual information into a format that intact senses can process. Here the translation is image-to-sound.

They tested localization of visual stimuli, LEDs and objects, using image-to-sound conversion in 13 blindfolded participants. The study separates effects of learning by doing from those of long-term sensory deprivation. The full text gives the accuracy results. Such devices could restore a measure of spatial awareness to blind users, and they test how flexibly the brain can remap one sense onto another.
plos-pone-0001940:
Zhaojie Li, Shicui Zhang, and Qinghui Liu reported a second job for a fish egg protein in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The protein, vitellogenin, is best known as a building material for eggs and new life. It had also been tied to defense against infection in fish, but no one knew how it helped.

The team tested how the protein meets microbes in the lab, using binding tests and enzyme-linked assays. They report that it works as a broad pattern sensor that flags germs, and that it helps immune cells engulf them. A food protein that also fights germs blurs the line between growth and defense.
plos-pone-0002040:
Adinda Wellens and co-authors designed germ blockers from the shape of a bacterial grip protein, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Certain Escherichia coli strains cling to the wall of the human urinary tract with hair-like pili. At the tip sits FimH, a protein that grips mannose sugars on the surface, and a few clinging bacteria can then invade bladder cells.

The team used the crystal structure of FimH bound to a mannose chain to build anti-adhesives, molecules that jam the grip. Blocking attachment, rather than killing the germ, could treat urinary infections with less pressure for drug resistance.
plos-pone-0002140:
Jianhua Xing and Jing Chen revisited a classic piece of math in cell biology, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. In 1981, Goldbeter and Koshland showed how a simple cycle of protein changes can act like a sharp switch. A small rise in a signal molecule can flip the system from nearly off to nearly on, giving a steep, S-shaped response curve.

Xing and Chen studied that switch in its first-order region, where the response is more gentle. Asked how it behaves when the cell's inner parts move in a noisy, disordered way. Their math shows how cells can stay sensitive to signals even when conditions inside are messy and always shifting.
plos-pone-0002240:
Andrew Pask, Richard Behringer, and Marilyn Renfree brought a piece of an extinct genome back to life in mice, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. DNA from extinct species can tell scientists how genomes evolved and what made each species distinct. Reading the code alone, though, cannot show what a gene actually did in a living animal.

The team took a DNA control element from an extinct marsupial genome. Placed in mice, it drove gene activity in the developing limb. Their test resurrected the function of DNA that no living species carries. The approach turns museum DNA into working biology, not just sequence.
plos-pone-0002340:
Lesley Rogers and Giorgio Vallortigara showed that honeybees recall a learned smell first on one side, then the other, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Bees, Apis mellifera, readily learn to link odors with sugar rewards. Recall is tested by the proboscis extension reflex: a bee that remembers sticks out its tongue at the trained odor.

The authors found that recall involves first the right antenna and then the left. Memory of the same odor shifts sides over time after learning. That lateral handover mirrors side specialization seen in vertebrate brains, and it suggests bees store the memory in stages, with each antenna taking its turn.
plos-pone-0002440:
Led by Kuehl, a team of researchers published its study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Hjalmar S. Kuehl, Caroline Elzner, Yasmin Moebius, and others. Its subject is the Price of Play: Self-Organized Infant Mortality Cycles in Chimpanzees. Chimpanzees have been used extensively as a model system for laboratory research on infectious diseases.

Ironically, we know next to nothing about disease dynamics in wild chimpanzee populations. Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time.
plos-pone-0002540:
Research by Leppänen and co-authors came out in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Olli V. Leppänen, Harri Sievänen, Jarkko Jokihaara, and others. Its subject is pathogenesis of Age-Related Osteoporosis: Impaired Mechano-Responsiveness of Bone Is Not the Culprit. According to prevailing understanding, skeletal mechano-responsiveness declines with age.

What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002640:
Work by Alison Maresh and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was principles of glomerular organization in the human olfactory bulb – implications for odor processing. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Alison Maresh, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Olfactory sensory neurons (OSN) in mice express only 1 of a possible 1. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002740:
Work by Rebecca Banerjee and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008, dealing with adaptive immune neuroprotection in G93A-SOD1 amyotrophic lateral sclerosis mice. The catalog record names Rebecca Banerjee first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Innate neuroimmune dysfunction is a pathobiological feature of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). The authors add a further point. However, links, if any, between disease and adaptive immunity are poorly understood. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002840:
Work by Katherine G. Akers and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was social competitiveness and plasticity of neuroendocrine function in old age: influence of neonatal novelty exposure and maternal care reliability. Authorship is credited in the record to Katherine G. Akers and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Early experience is known to have a profound impact on brain and behavioral function later in life. The authors add a further point. Relatively few studies, however, have examined whether the effects of early experience remain detectable in the aging animal. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002940:
Gregory Mullen, Ruth Ellis, Kazutoyo Miura and co-authors ran a first human trial of a malaria vaccine mix in 2008. The vaccine targets AMA1, a surface protein of the malaria parasite's blood stage, and pairs it with the adjuvant CPG 7909 to boost response. AMA1 was a leading blood-stage candidate.

This phase 1 trial in PLOS ONE tested safety and immune response for the AMA1 vaccine on Alhydrogel plus the new adjuvant. Phase 1 is the earliest human stage, focused on safety. Malaria vaccine research needs such careful steps, since blood-stage infection is what makes people ill.
plos-pone-0003040:
Héctor Guidobaldi, María Teves, Diego Uñates and co-authors identified the sperm attractant from rabbit egg complexes in 2008. Mammalian sperm swim toward several female sources, including follicular fluid and the cumulus cells around the egg. Several substances had been confirmed as attractants, and progesterone was a candidate.

Progesterone from the cumulus cells is the chemoattractant secreted by the rabbit oocyte cumulus complex, the title reports. Published in PLOS ONE, pinning the signal to one hormone from one source clarifies the final guidance step in fertilization. It may inform fertility testing and treatment. Details of samples, measures, and analysis are set out in the full article text.
plos-pone-0003140: Mady Hornig and colleagues published a case-control study in PLOS ONE in 2008 on measles vaccine and autism. The title states the result in plain terms: no link was found between measles virus vaccine and autism with enteropathy, a gut condition, in the group studied. No abstract beyond the title was supplied, so no study details are added here.
plos-pone-0003240:
Zoe T. Richards, Madeleine J. H. van Oppen, Carden C. Wallace and colleagues test whether rare corals are hybrids in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Coral reefs worldwide face a variety of threats, and many coral species are increasingly endangered. It is often assumed that rare coral species face higher extinction risks because they have very small effective population sizes, with decreased genetic diversity as a predicted consequence.

The title reports that some rare Indo-Pacific coral species are probable hybrids. Readers learn that rarity can reflect origin, not just decline. If a rare coral is a hybrid, its conservation value and protection strategy need fresh thought.
plos-pone-0003340:
Yanlin Shi, Qilong Xu, Sunita V. Seemanaplli and colleagues study Lyme disease proteins in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. As an extracellular bacterium, the Lyme disease spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi resides in the extracellular matrix and connective tissues. It also sits between host cells during infection of mammals. Decorin and glycosaminoglycans are found in plenty in those places. Its ties to those materials are thus central.

The authors assess common and unique contributions of decorin-binding proteins A and B to overall virulence of Borrelia burgdorferi. Readers learn how two similar binding proteins divide work in infection. Adhesion proteins are targets because blocking attachment can prevent disease without killing bacteria directly.
plos-pone-0007440: Multiple sclerosis varies wildly between patients, so doctors want a blood test that can flag the disease early. This study read the patterns of tiny regulatory molecules called microRNAs and found they cleanly separated patients with relapsing-remitting MS from healthy people. A reliable microRNA signature could become a practical tool for diagnosis.
plos-pone-0007540: People with Down syndrome seem oddly protected from artery disease, and a gene called DYRK1A may explain why. In mice carrying extra copies of this Down-syndrome-linked gene, the researchers found it controls the methionine-homocysteine cycle, whose imbalance raises heart risk. The gene emerges as a lever on a key metabolic pathway.
plos-pone-0007640: Kinetochores are the handles by which chromosomes are pulled apart during cell division. This study dissected a conserved protein complex, Spc105p/Kre28p, in yeast and showed it anchors microtubules to the kinetochore and enforces the spindle checkpoint. The finding details a critical joint in the cell-division machinery.
plos-pone-0007740: A hospital germ's family map got redrawn. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Pirnay's team re-examined Pseudomonas aeruginosa population structure. Clinic and soil isolates looked alike. The epidemic-structure case was mapped. The redraw feeds infection control.
plos-pone-0007840: A transfusion of donor blood before a liver transplant can teach the body to accept the organ. This rat study showed the tolerance requires Foxp3 regulatory T cells induced by the transfusion. The finding charts a drug-free path to transplant acceptance.
plos-pone-0007940: America wastes more food every year, and the waste carries a climate cost. This study calculated the energy content of the nation's food waste and its burden in freshwater, fossil fuel, and emissions. The numbers put a price tag on what we throw away.
plos-pone-0008040: Liver cell signaling was modeled as a discrete logic circuit. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Wu and colleagues applied discrete modeling to IRS-PKR signaling in liver cells. Systems biology needs dynamic understanding of networks, not just static maps. The discrete approach captures the signaling behavior without heavy equations.
plos-pone-0008140: The lumpy skins of proteins got a quicker measuring tape. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Xu and Zhang built triangulated molecular surfaces using the Euclidean distance transform. Accurate surfaces are the starting point for docking drugs into proteins and for virtual screening, but computing them is costly. The new method races through the math without losing detail. Faster surfaces mean faster structure-based drug design.
plos-pone-0008240: A bacterial iron hook was found disarming immune cells. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Paauw's team showed yersiniabactin blunts the oxidative burst of innate immune cells. The siderophore, encoded on a high-pathogenicity island, steals iron to fuel bacterial growth. Robbing iron also quiets the immune counterattack. The double duty helps explain the island's virulence boost.
plos-pone-0008340: Stripping DNA methylation made tumors nastier. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Hamm's team treated rat cartilage-tumor cells with a demethylating drug and watched tumorigenicity rise. Losing methylation genome-wide had unknown effects. The global wipe made the cells more aggressive. The result warns that epigenetic drugs can backfire.
plos-pone-0008440: People living in high natural radiation areas offered a test of telomere effects. This study compared telomere length in adults exposed to background radiation. The in vivo data test whether chronic low-dose radiation ages chromosomes.
plos-pone-0008540: A bacterial sidekick was tied to worse pandemic flu. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Palacios's team tied Streptococcus pneumoniae co-infection to deadlier H1N1 cases. Argentina's death-rate spike needed explaining. The bacterial partner emerged as the suspect. The link argues for germ-fighting drugs in severe flu. The result may reshape flu care.
plos-pone-0008640: A plant gas's dock sites got caught clustering. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Chen's team found the mustard-weed's ethylene dock sites clump into big groups. The five-part family sticks together. The clump pattern was mapped. The clustering hints at signal design.
plos-pone-0008740: C. difficile's wake-up call got traced to bile. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Giel's team showed mouse bile-salt metabolism triggers Clostridium difficile spore germination. The gut-chemistry cue was mapped. The trace suggests prevention angles.
plos-pone-0008840: Alzheimer's mice got a memory rescue. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Ha's team showed S100a9 knockdown decreases memory impairment and neuropathology in Tg2576 Alzheimer's mice. The inflammatory gene's silencing was tested. The rescue suggests therapy targets.
plos-pone-0008940: Field disease notes got a gene-reading lens. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Bishop and Woolliams wrote rules for reading genes from field disease notes. The farm-data rules were set down clearly. The lens aids herd and flock science.
plos-pone-0009040: Preterm birth got a mother-baby gene hunt. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Ryckman's team tested maternal and fetal PTGER3 and PON1 variants for preterm birth links. The Norwegian cohort's associations were mapped. The hunt informs obstetrics.
plos-pone-0009140: Heart-muscle disease got a double-mutant model. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Davis and Metzger combined two cardiomyopathy mutant alleles in rodent myocytes to model myofilament dysregulation. The combinatorial effects were mapped. The model informs cardiac genetics.
plos-pone-0009240: A worm's entire nervous system was analyzed as a network. This 2010 PLOS ONE study by Pan and colleagues examined the mesoscopic organization of the Caenorhabditis elegans nervous system to reveal the constraints governing it. Bridging cellular activity and whole-organism behavior, the network analysis shows how the wiring's intermediate-scale structure shapes responses to stimuli. The complete connectome makes such analysis possible.
plos-pone-0009340: Heart risk got a pee-test warning. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Montine's team tied pee-test ratios to heart events. The pee warning was logged. The warning feeds drug safety. The ratios predict events in trials.
plos-pone-0011440: Teenagers chase rewards harder than adults do — but what differs in their brains? This research paper uses fMRI brain scans to compare how adolescents and adults recruit motivational circuitry when rewards are on the line. Mapping the neural gap behind teenage risk-taking gives parents, teachers, and policymakers a brain-based view of why adolescence feels so impulsive.
plos-pone-0011540: Cells proofread their RNA, junking messages with faulty splice sites. This research paper shows that in yeast, such defective RNAs are held in the nucleus by Rrp6 and the faulty genes get dialed down. The quality-control circuit reveals how cells quarantine bad transcripts before they can do harm.
plos-pone-0011640: Rhesus macaques with SIV are the closest animal model of AIDS. This research paper measures how fast the virus decays in their blood once highly active antiretroviral therapy begins. The decay kinetics reveal the lifespan of infected cells, informing treatment strategies for humans.
plos-pone-0011740: PDCD10 is a protein tied to programmed cell death and brain vessel malformations. This research paper maps its functional domain by studying how it grips PIP3, a key membrane lipid. The binding map shows which part of the protein does the work — a foothold for understanding its role in disease.
plos-pone-0011840: Cheap short DNA reads choke on tangled microbe communities. This research paper cracks the problem, unlocking short-read sequencing for whole-community studies. The fix brings affordable sequencing to Earth's microbial majority — the unseen life thriving all around us every day.
plos-pone-0011940: Muscles remodel constantly, and calpain 3 is a key switch. This research paper shows it acts as a rapid, one-way proteolytic switch central to muscle remodeling. The switch discovery reveals the demolition crew behind muscle renewal and repair every day.
plos-pone-0012040: XMRV was once blamed for diseases — but is it even there? This research paper reports no detection of XMRV in seminal plasma from HIV-1 infected men in the Netherlands. The negative result further deflates the XMRV scare for good, finally.
plos-pone-0012140: An SMA trial tests L-carnitine plus valproic acid. This double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial (CARNI-VAL Part I) tests the combo in spinal muscular atrophy. The rigorous trial reveals whether the combo helps young patients with SMA today.
